Job declares his integrity (verses 1–8)

Job was not boasting.

He was answering accusations of hypocrisy.

He understood that God's commands reach beyond outward actions into the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

Normally our conduct should speak for itself.

But when serious false charges threaten both our reputation and God's cause, there are times when we ought solemnly to protest our innocence.

Two dangers have ruined countless people: sinful bodily desires and love of the world.

Job had watched carefully against both.

God examines us even more closely than we examine ourselves.

We should therefore live carefully.

Job avoided dishonest ways of gaining wealth.

He feared forbidden profit as much as forbidden pleasure.

We can use our possessions with comfort, or lose them without disgrace, when they were honestly gained.

Without strict honesty and faithfulness in business and relationships, we have no sound evidence of genuine godliness.

Yet many who profess faith cannot pass this test.

Job defends his conduct toward his household (verses 9–15)

The sins that pollute a life arise from a heart that has been deceived.

Lust is like a fire burning within.

When people indulge it, it consumes what is good in the soul and leaves the conscience ruined.

It kindles the fire of God's wrath, which will consume even to eternal destruction unless quenched by the blood of Christ.

It may also destroy the body and waste a person's possessions.

Burning desires bring burning judgments.

Job had managed a large household.

He remembered that he too had a Master in heaven.

If God treated us with the strictness we deserve, we would be ruined.

Therefore we should treat everyone entrusted to our care with gentleness and fairness.

Job speaks about mercy toward the poor (verses 16–23)

Job's conscience bore witness to his charitable and just treatment of poor people.

He spoke particularly at length about this because his friends had accused him directly of oppressing them.

He had sought to be tender toward everyone and harmful to no one.

What restrained him from cruelty and lack of compassion?

He feared the Lord and knew that God would oppose him if he harmed the poor.

Concern for worldly reputation may restrain people from committing visible offenses.

But God's grace alone can make them truly hate, fear and avoid sinful thoughts and desires.

Job rejects greed, idolatry and malice (verses 24–32)

Job made four denials.

First, he had never set his heart upon worldly wealth.

How few prosperous people who profess religion can sincerely say they never rejoiced merely because their wealth increased!

The determination to become rich can ruin souls and pierce lives with sorrow.

Second, Job had not practiced idolatry.

Its source lies in the heart, and it corrupts people and brings judgment on communities.

Third, he had never wished harm upon an enemy or taken delight in an enemy's misfortune.

Another person's hatred does not justify our hatred.

Fourth, he had never been unkind to strangers.

Hospitality is a Christian duty (1 Peter 4:9).

Job rejects hypocrisy and injustice (verses 33–40)

Job denied the charge of hypocrisy.

Human beings are reluctant to confess wrong, eager to make excuses and inclined to blame others.

But people who cover their sins will not prosper (Proverbs 28:13).

Job cited his courage in doing right as evidence of sincerity.

People who acquire wealth unjustly may rightly lose every comfort they expected from it.

Their field may be sown with wheat, but the crop will be thistles.

What is not honestly obtained can never bring lasting good.

Here Job's speeches ended.

He concluded with a strong appeal to God concerning the accusations against his moral and religious character.

But despite Job's confidence, we will later see that he was mistaken in some of his claims (Job 40:4–5; 1 John 1:8).

Let us all examine ourselves.

Where we have sinned, seek pardon through the blood of Jesus Christ, which cleanses us from every sin.

May God have mercy on us and write his law upon our hearts.

[Job.31.1-Job.31.8]
Chapter 31
Chapter Outline
Job declares his uprightness. | (1-8) |
His integrity. | (9-15) |
Job merciful. | (16-23) |
Job not guilty of covetousness or idolatry. | (24-32) |
Job not guilty of hypocrisy and violence. | (33-40) |
Verses 1-8
Job did not speak the things here recorded by way of boasting, but in answer to the charge of hypocrisy. He understood the spiritual nature of God's commandments, as reaching to the thoughts and intents of the heart. It is best to let our actions speak for us; but in some cases we owe it to ourselves and to the cause of God, solemnly to protest our innocence of the crimes of which we are falsely accused. The lusts of the flesh, and the love of the world, are two fatal rocks on which multitudes split; against these Job protests he was always careful to stand upon his guard. And God takes more exact notice of us than we do of ourselves; let us therefore walk circumspectly. He carefully avoided all sinful means of getting wealth. He dreaded all forbidden profit as much as all forbidden pleasure. What we have in the world may be used with comfort, or lost with comfort, if honestly gotten. Without strict honestly and faithfulness in all our dealings, we can have no good evidence of true godliness. Yet how many professors are unable to abide this touchstone!
[Job.31.9-Job.31.15]
Verses 9-15
All the defilements of the life come from a deceived heart. Lust is a fire in the soul: those that indulge it, are said to burn. It consumes all that is good there, and lays the conscience waste. It kindles the fire of God's wrath, which, if not quenched by the blood of Christ, will consume even to eternal destruction. It consumes the body; it consumes the substance. Burning lusts bring burning judgments. Job had a numerous household, and he managed it well. He considered that he had a Master in heaven; and as we are undone if God should be severe with us, we ought to be mild and gentle towards all with whom we have to do.
[Job.31.16-Job.31.23]
Verses 16-23
Job's conscience gave testimony concerning his just and charitable behaviour toward the poor. He is most large upon this head, because in this matter he was particularly accused. He was tender of all, and hurtful to none. Notice the principles by which Job was restrained from being uncharitable and unmerciful. He stood in awe of the Lord, as certainly against him, if he should wrong the poor. Regard to worldly interests may restrain a man from actual crimes; but the grace of God alone can make him hate, dread, and shun sinful thoughts and desires.
[Job.31.24-Job.31.32]
Verses 24-32
Job protests, 1. That he never set his heart upon the wealth of this world. How few prosperous professors can appeal to the Lord, that they have not rejoiced because their gains were great! Through the determination to be rich, numbers ruin their souls, or pierce themselves with many sorrows. 2. He never was guilty of idolatry. The source of idolatry is in the heart, and it corrupts men, and provokes God to send judgments upon a nation. 3. He neither desired nor delighted in the hurt of the worst enemy he had. If others bear malice to us, that will not justify us in bearing malice to them. 4. He had never been unkind to strangers. Hospitality is a Christian duty, [1Pet.4.9] 1Pe 4:9.
[Job.31.33-Job.31.40]
Verses 33-40
Job clears himself from the charge of hypocrisy. We are loth to confess our faults, willing to excuse them, and to lay the blame upon others. But he that thus covers his sins, shall not prosper, [Prov.28.13] Pr 28:13. He speaks of his courage in what is good, as an evidence of his sincerity in it. When men get estates unjustly, they are justly deprived of comfort from them; it was sown wheat, but shall come up thistles. What men do not come honestly by, will never do them any good. The words of Job are ended. They end with a bold assertion, that, with respect to accusation against his moral and religious character as the cause for his sufferings, he could appeal to God. But, however confident Job was, we shall see he was mistaken, chap. 40:4, 5; [1John.1.8] 1Jo 1:8. Let us all judge ourselves; wherein we are guilty, let us seek forgiveness in that blood which cleanseth from all sin; and may the Lord have mercy upon us, and write his laws in our hearts!

Elihu is distressed by the argument (verses 1–5)

Job's friends had stopped speaking, but they were not persuaded.

Other people had been listening.

Elihu was rightly displeased with Job for being more eager to clear his own reputation than to defend God's justice and goodness.

He was also displeased with Job's friends because they had not treated Job fairly.

Few quarrels begin—and even fewer continue—without some wrongdoing on both sides.

People who seek truth must not reject what is right in either party's arguments or defend what is wrong in either one.

Elihu corrects both parties (verses 6–14)

Elihu professed to speak under the Holy Spirit's inspiration and sought to correct both Job and his friends.

He recognized that older people with more experience should normally speak first.

Yet God distributes wisdom as he chooses.

This gave Elihu courage to express his view.

Through careful attention to God's word and dependence upon the Holy Spirit, young people may become wiser than older people.

But real wisdom makes them quick to listen, slow to speak and willing to hear others patiently.

Elihu speaks without flattery (verses 15–22)

Even if we are convinced the Holy Spirit has given us something valuable to say, we should wait for the proper opportunity.

God brings order, not confusion.

A faithful person finds refreshment in speaking for God's glory and helping others grow in faith.

The more we contemplate the majesty of God our Maker, and the more we fear his wrath and justice, the less we will fear or flatter people.

If we keep the Lord's mercy and the terrors of his wrath before us, we can remain steady in whatever duty he assigns us.

[Job.32.1-Job.32.5]
Chapter 32
Chapter Outline
Elihu is displeased at the dispute between Job and his friends. | (1-5) |
He reproves them. | (6-14) |
He speaks without partiality. | (15-22) |
Verses 1-5
Job's friends were silenced, but not convinced. Others had been present. Elihu was justly displeased with Job, as more anxious to clear his own character than the justice and goodness of God. Elihu was displeased with Job's friends because they had not been candid to Job. Seldom is a quarrel begun, more seldom is a quarrel carried on, in which there are not faults on both sides. Those that seek for truth, must not reject what is true and good on either side, nor approve or defend what is wrong.
[Job.32.6-Job.32.14]
Verses 6-14
Elihu professes to speak by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and corrects both parties. He allowed that those who had the longest experience should speak first. But God gives wisdom as he pleases; this encouraged him to state his opinion. By attention to the word of God, and dependence upon the Holy Spirit, young men may become wiser than the aged; but this wisdom will render them swift to hear, slow to speak, and disposed to give others a patient hearing.
[Job.32.15-Job.32.22]
Verses 15-22
If we are sure that the Spirit of God suggested what we are about to say, still we ought to refrain, till it comes to our turn to speak. God is the God of order, not of confusion. It is great refreshment to a good man, to speak for the glory of the Lord, and to edify others. And the more we consider the majesty of God, as our Maker, and the more we dread his wrath and justice, the less shall we sinfully fear or flatter men. Could we set the wrath Lord always before us, in his mercies and his terrors, we should not be moved from doing our duty in whatever we are called to do.

Elihu offers to reason with Job (verses 1–7)

Job had wanted an impartial judge to hear his case.

In one sense Elihu was an answer to that request: he was another human being like Job.

To persuade people rightly, we must use reason rather than terror, fair arguments rather than force.

Elihu corrects Job's accusations against God (verses 8–13)

Elihu charged Job with speaking against God's justice and goodness.

When we hear statements that dishonor God, we should testify against them.

Job had described God as harshly recording his wrongs.

Elihu said he had spoken improperly and ought to humble himself and withdraw those accusations through repentance.

God is not accountable to human beings.

It is unreasonable for weak and sinful creatures to quarrel with the infinitely wise, powerful and good God.

He acts with perfect justice, wisdom and goodness, even when we cannot see the reasons.

God calls people to repentance (verses 14–18)

God speaks through conscience, Providence and ministers.

Elihu considered all three.

At that time, Henry says, no written divine revelation was known to be available; written Scripture is now our principal guide.

When God intends a person's good, he may use inward conviction to open the heart, as he opened Lydia's heart, and open the ears so that a warning is heard.

These messages aim to keep people from sin, especially pride.

Sinners who indulge sinful plans and pride are moving toward destruction.

Turning them away from sin saves them from hell.

An awakened conscience that restrains sin is a great mercy.

God uses affliction for the soul's good (verses 19–28)

Job concluded from his illness that God was angry with him.

His friends made the same assumption.

Elihu explained that God often afflicts the body for the good of the soul.

Understanding this can help us respond wisely to sickness as a means by which God speaks.

Pain entered the world through sin.

Yet through divine grace, bodily suffering can help the soul.

When an affliction has accomplished its purpose, it may be removed.

A ransom or atoning sacrifice has been found.

Henry identifies Jesus Christ as both the Messenger and the Ransom of which Elihu speaks, just as Job had called him his Redeemer.

Christ is both the One who purchases redemption and its price, the Priest and the Sacrifice.

A human soul is so valuable, and sin has brought such ruin, that nothing less than the blood of God's Son could provide redemption.

He gave his life as a ransom for many.

When recovery from illness follows forgiveness of sin, that recovery is especially precious.

Everyone who truly repents will find mercy with God.

The works of darkness bear no good fruit.

Sin's apparent gains are much less than the harm it brings.

We must confess sin to God with a broken and humble heart (1 John 1:9).

Confession has three parts.

First, acknowledge the fact of sin rather than making excuses.

Second, acknowledge its wrongness: I have distorted what is right.

Third, acknowledge its folly: I acted foolishly and without understanding.

We have every reason to confess this way.

Elihu asks Job to listen (verses 29–33)

Elihu taught that God's gracious purpose toward human beings is to rescue them from everlasting misery and bring them into lasting happiness.

Whatever he uses to turn us away from ruin deserves our thanksgiving, even when the experience itself is painful.

Those who finally perish are without excuse because they refused the healing offered to them.

[Job.33.1-Job.33.7]
Chapter 33
Chapter Outline
Elihu offers to reason with Job. | (1-7) |
Elihu blames Job for reflecting upon God. | (8-13) |
God calls men to repentance. | (14-18) |
God sends afflictions for good. | (19-28) |
Elihu entreats Job's attention. | (29-33) |
Verses 1-7
Job had desired a judge to decide his appeal. Elihu was one according to his wish, a man like himself. If we would rightly convince men, it must be by reason, not by terror; by fair argument, not by a heavy hand.
[Job.33.8-Job.33.13]
Verses 8-13
Elihu charges Job with reflecting upon the justice and goodness of God. When we hear any thing said to God's dishonour, we ought to bear our testimony against it. Job had represented God as severe in marking what he did amiss. Elihu urges that he had spoken wrong, and that he ought to humble himself before God, and by repentance to unsay it. God is not accountable to us. It is unreasonable for weak, sinful creatures, to strive with a God of infinite wisdom, power, and goodness. He acts with perfect justice, wisdom, and goodness, where we cannot perceive it.
[Job.33.14-Job.33.18]
Verses 14-18
God speaks to us by conscience, by providences, and by ministers; of all these Elihu discourses. There was not then, that we know of, any Divine revelation in writing, though now it is our principal guide. When God designs men's good, by the convictions and dictates of their own consciences, he opens the heart, as Lydia's, and opens the ears, so that conviction finds or forces its way in. The end and design of these admonitions are to keep men from sin, particularly the sin of pride. While sinners are pursuing evil purposes, and indulging their pride, their souls are hastening to destruction. That which turns men from sin, saves them from hell. What a mercy it is to be under the restraints of an awakened conscience!
[Job.33.19-Job.33.28]
Verses 19-28
Job complained of his diseases, and judged by them that God was angry with him; his friends did so too: but Elihu shows that God often afflicts the body for good to the soul. This thought will be of great use for our getting good from sickness, in and by which God speaks to men. Pain is the fruit of sin; yet, by the grace of God, the pain of the body is often made a means of good to the soul. When afflictions have done their work, they shall be removed. A ransom or propitiation is found. Jesus Christ is the Messenger and the Ransom, so Elihu calls him, as Job had called him his Redeemer, for he is both the Purchaser and the Price, the Priest and the sacrifice. So high was the value of souls, that nothing less would redeem them; and so great the hurt done by sin, that nothing less would atone for it, than the blood of the Son of God, who gave his life a ransom for many. A blessed change follows. Recovery from sickness is a mercy indeed, when it proceeds from the remission of sin. All that truly repent of their sins, shall find mercy with God. The works of darkness are unfruitful works; all the gains of sin will come far short of the damage. We must, with a broken and contrite heart, confess our sins to God, [1John.1.9] 1Jo 1:9. We must confess the fact of sin; and not try to justify or excuse ourselves. We must confess the fault of sin; I have perverted that which was right. We must confess the folly of sin; So foolish have I been and ignorant. Is there not good reason why we should make such a confession?
[Job.33.29-Job.33.33]
Verses 29-33
Elihu shows that God's great and gracious design toward the children of men, is, to save them from being for ever miserable, and to bring them to be for ever happy. By whatever means we are kept back from the we shall bless the Lord for them at least, and should bless him for them though they be painful and distressing. Those that perish for ever are without excuse, for they would not be healed.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesElihu accuses Job of charging God with injustice.1–9God cannot be unjust.10–15God's power and providence.16–30Elihu reproves Job.31–37
Elihu calls for judgment on Job's words (verses 1–9)

Elihu invited the people present to consider Job's words with him and determine what was right.

An ordinary Christian whose mind has been enlightened, whose heart has been sanctified by God's Spirit, and who knows Scripture can often judge whether a belief, statement or action agrees with true religion better than someone depending only on personal understanding.

Job had spoken as though he intended to justify himself completely.

Someone who says, “I have kept my hands clean for nothing,” offends God's children and speaks in agreement with God's enemies rather than his friends (Psalm 73:13–15).

God cannot act unjustly (verses 10–15)

Elihu had already explained that God did not intend to harm Job through his suffering.

Rather, he intended Job's spiritual good.

Now Elihu argued that God did him no wrong in afflicting him.

If knowing God's good purpose did not satisfy Job, remembering God's justice should have silenced his complaints.

The Almighty never does evil or injustice.

Some faithful service remains unrewarded in this life, and some sins seem to go unpunished.

But the day of judgment is coming, when God will repay everyone according to their works.

A believer cannot be finally condemned, because the Savior has paid the ransom.

Even so, our sins deserve far worse than any outward suffering we experience, so no injustice is done when God tests us severely.

God's rule is righteous and complete (verses 16–30)

Elihu appealed directly to Job.

Could he seriously imagine that God resembles unjust earthly rulers who hate righteousness and become scourges to those they govern?

It is presumptuous to condemn God's ways because we dislike our circumstances.

Elihu reminded Job of God's greatness and sovereignty so that he would submit.

Job had often wanted to bring his case personally before God.

What could he accomplish by doing so?

Everything God does is right, and eventually it will be seen to be so.

A soul resting securely in God cannot be made truly miserable by worldly troubles.

But the approval of the whole world cannot comfort a person who remains under God's displeasure.

Elihu corrects Job's complaints (verses 31–37)

When we rebuke someone for doing wrong, we must also show the person what would be right.

Job's friends had demanded that he confess to being a wicked man.

Elihu instead urged Job to acknowledge that he had spoken rashly and unwisely.

We should not exaggerate another person's fault when correcting it.

Elihu taught Job to humble himself, accept God's discipline and pray to discover whatever sins needed to be addressed.

A godly person is willing to know even unpleasant truths about personal faults.

Especially in suffering, a believer wants to understand why God is contending with him.

It is not enough to regret sin: we must turn away from it.

Children who love their father are willing to speak honestly with him and open their minds to him.

We often want everything concerning us to happen exactly as we planned, but that expectation is unreasonable.

Job should ask whether his complaints revealed sin and folly.

The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works (Psalm 145:17).

A believer may therefore say: Let my Savior, my wise and loving Lord, choose everything for me. His choice will be the wisest, bringing the greatest glory to him and the most lasting good to me.

[Job.34.1-Job.34.9]
Chapter 34
Chapter Outline
Elihu accuses Job of charging God with injustice. | (1-9) |
God cannot be unjust. | (10-15) |
God's power and providence. | (16-30) |
Elihu reproves Job. | (31-37) |
Verses 1-9
Elihu calls upon those present to decide with him upon Job's words. The plainest Christian, whose mind is enlightened, whose heart is sanctified by the Spirit of God, and who is versed in the Scriptures, can say how far matters, words, or actions, agree with true religion, better than any that lean to their own understandings. Job had spoken as if he meant wholly to justify himself. He that say, I have cleansed my hands in vain, does not only offend against God's children, [Ps.73.13-Ps.73.15] Psa 73:13-15, but gratifies his enemies, and says as they say.
[Job.34.10-Job.34.15]
Verses 10-15
Elihu had showed Job, that God meant him no hurt by afflicting him, but intended his spiritual benefit. Here he shows, that God did him no wrong by afflicting him. If the former did not satisfy him, this ought to silence him. God cannot do wickedness, nor the Almighty commit wrong. If services now go unrewarded, and sins now go unpunished, yet there is a day coming, when God will fully render to every man according to his works. Further, though the believer's final condemnation is done away through the Saviour's ransom, yet he has merited worse than any outward afflictions; so that no wrong is done to him, however he may be tried.
[Job.34.16-Job.34.30]
Verses 16-30
Elihu appeals directly to Job himself. Could he suppose that God was like those earthly princes, who hate right, who are unfit to rule, and prove the scourges of mankind? It is daring presumption to condemn God's proceedings, as Job had done by his discontents. Elihu suggests divers considerations to Job, to produce in him high thoughts of God, and so to persuade him to submit. Job had often wished to plead his cause before God. Elihu asks, To what purpose? All is well that God does, and will be found so. What can make those uneasy, whose souls dwell at ease in God? The smiles of all the world cannot quiet those on whom God frowns.
[Job.34.31-Job.34.37]
Verses 31-37
When we reprove for what is amiss, we must direct to what is good. Job's friends would have had him own himself a wicked man. Let will only oblige him to own that he spoke unadvisedly with his lips. Let us, in giving reproof, not make a matter worse than it is. Elihu directs Job to humble himself before God for his sins, and to accept the punishment. Also to pray to God to discover his sins to him. A good man is willing to know the worst of himself; particularly, under affliction, he desires to be told wherefore God contends with him. It is not enough to be sorry for our sins, but we must go and sin no more. And if we are affectionate children, we shall love to speak with our Father, and to tell him all our mind. Elihu reasons with Job concerning his discontent under affliction. We are ready to think every thing that concerns us should be just as we would have it; but it is not reasonable to expect this. Elihu asks whether there was not sin and folly in what Job said. God is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works, [Ps.145.17] Psa 145:17. The believer saith, Let my Saviour, my wise and loving Lord, choose every thing for me. I am sure that will be wisest, and the best for his glory and my good.

Our conduct cannot enrich God (verses 1–8)

Elihu reproved Job for caring more about his own justification than God's honor.

He directed Job's attention to the heavens.

They stand far above us, and God is infinitely greater still.

Neither human sins nor our faithful service can diminish or enrich him as though he depended on us.

We have no reason to complain when God does not give everything we hoped to receive.

Instead, we should be thankful that he has already given more good than we deserve.

Why some cries during suffering go unanswered (verses 9–13)

Job had wondered why God did not intervene when oppressed people cried out against their oppressors.

He found this difficult to reconcile with God's justice.

Elihu answered that people often ignore the mercies they receive during their suffering.

Instead of recognizing and thanking the Lord for these blessings, they focus entirely on their trouble.

God gives songs in the night.

When our circumstances are dark and sorrowful, his providence and promises offer enough comfort to strengthen us and even make us rejoice amid trials.

If we refuse the consolations God offers and attend only to what we have lost, we have no right to demand that he answer every prayer as we wish.

Events that kill the body cannot destroy the soul.

When God has not removed an affliction, it does not follow that his arm lacks power or his ear cannot hear.

Elihu taught that the sufferer may still need to be humbled.

This is Elihu's explanation in the present dispute, not a license to assume that every unanswered plea for relief proves a particular sin in another sufferer.

Elihu corrects Job's impatience (verses 14–16)

During prosperity we may imagine our mountain will never be moved.

During suffering we may imagine the valley will never be filled.

But expecting tomorrow to resemble today is as foolish as thinking that fair or stormy weather will last forever.

Job had no reason to despair when looking to God.

A day of final judgment is coming.

Then what appears wrong will be seen in the light of divine justice, and what is dark or difficult will be understood.

Henry says that if divine wrath is present in our troubles, it is because we quarrel with God, grow fretful and distrust his Providence.

He applies this diagnosis to Job.

Elihu was directed by God to humble Job, because Job had spoken rashly about matters beyond his knowledge.

When we suffer, we should not speak only of how great our pain is.

We should also consider and praise how great God's mercy is.
classic_reading:
[Job.35.1-Job.35.8]
Chapter 35
Chapter Outline
Elihu speaks of man's conduct. | (1-8) |
Why those who cry out under afflictions are not regarded. | (9-13) |
Elihu reproves Job's impatience. | (14-16) |
Verses 1-8
Elihu reproves Job for justifying himself more than God, and called his attention to the heavens. They are far above us, and God is far above them; how much then is he out of the reach, either of our sins or of our services! We have no reason to complain if we have not what we expect, but should be thankful that we have better than we deserve.
[Job.35.9-Job.35.13]
Verses 9-13
Job complained that God did not regard the cries of the oppressed against their oppressors. This he knew not how to reconcile the justice of God and his government. Elihu solves the difficulty. Men do not notice the mercies they enjoy in and under their afflictions, nor are thankful for them, therefore they cannot expect that God should deliver them out of affliction. He gives songs in the night; when our condition is dark and melancholy, there is that in God's providence and promise, which is sufficient to support us, and to enable us even to rejoice in tribulation. When we only pore upon our afflictions, and neglect the consolations of God which are treasured up for us, it is just in God to reject our prayers. Even the things that will kill the body, cannot hurt the soul. If we cry to God for the removal of an affliction, and it is not removed, the reason is, not because the Lord's hand is shortened, or his ear heavy; but because we are not sufficiently humbled.
[Job.35.14-Job.35.16]
Verses 14-16
As in prosperity we are ready to think our mountain will never be brought low; so when in adversity, we are ready to think our valley will never be filled up. But to conclude that to-morrow must be as this day, is as absurd as to think that the weather, when either fair or foul, will be always so. When Job looked up to God, he had no reason to speak despairingly. There is a day of judgment, when all that seems amiss will be found to be right, and all that seems dark and difficult will be cleared up and set straight. And if there is Divine wrath in our troubles, it is because we quarrel with God, are fretful, and distrust Divine Providence. This was Job's case. God's power displayed in weather (verses 1–13)

Changes in the weather occupy much of our thinking and conversation.

Yet how seldom do we speak about them as Elihu did—with reverence toward God, who directs them!

We should recognize his glory not only in frightening thunder and lightning, but also in ordinary, quieter changes such as snow and rain.

Animals instinctively seek refuge when a storm comes.

Should humans alone remain without a shelter?

God warns people in many ways to flee from the wrath to come.

He also invites them to receive his salvation and be happy.

People reveal how little they trust divine Providence by the way they complain about the weather.

The outcome of an entire year often shows how foolish those complaints were.

Believers should avoid this pattern.

No day is made evil by the Lord.

We make many days miserable through our own sin.

Job cannot fully explain God's works (verses 14–20)

Thinking carefully about God's works in nature can reconcile our hearts to the events of his Providence.

God sends both the freezing north wind and the warm, thawing south wind.

The Holy Spirit is compared with both because he convicts and comforts (Song of Songs 4:16).

Even the best human beings understand little about God's glorious character and government.

People who through grace know much about God still know almost nothing compared with everything that remains to be known.

How much greater will our knowledge be when what is perfect has come!

God's greatness and the clouds over human understanding (verses 21–24)

Elihu concluded with statements about God's majesty.

Sunlight continues shining even when clouds hide it.

In the same way, the light of God's favor continues toward his faithful servants even when they cannot perceive it.

Sin can come between our hearts and that comforting light.

Sorrow can also darken our minds.

But God has a wind that can scatter the clouds: the Holy Spirit.

As a wind sweeps clouds across the sky, God's Spirit removes the ignorance, unbelief, sin and harmful desires clouding the soul through regeneration.

The Spirit also removes the clouds that trouble a believer's conscience through consolation.

Now that the Lord was about to speak for himself, Elihu summed up his discourse.

With God is majestic and awe-inspiring power.

Sooner or later, every human being will fear him.

The Lord calls Job to answer (verses 1–3)

Job had silenced his friends but had not persuaded them.

Elihu had silenced Job without bringing him to acknowledge his fault before God.

Now the Lord himself intervened.

God humbled Job and brought him to repent of the passionate words he had spoken about divine Providence.

The Lord did so by setting a series of contrasts before him:

God lives forever, while Job's life is brief.

God knows everything, while Job's knowledge is limited.

God possesses almighty strength, while Job is weak.

It seriously offends God when human folly obscures the counsel of his wisdom.

Humble faith and sincere obedience give us the clearest understanding of his will.

God questions Job about earth and sea (verses 4–11)

To humble Job, God showed that he knew so little even about the earth and the sea.

We are not qualified to find fault with God's work.

Nor need we fear that his work will fail.

The works of his Providence and creation are secure.

So is the work of redemption, whose foundation and cornerstone is Jesus Christ.

God's church rests on a foundation as firm as the earth.

Light, darkness and our ignorance (verses 12–24)

The Lord challenged Job to recognize the extent of what he did not know.

When we examine ourselves in this way, we discover how little our knowledge is compared with everything unknown to us.

Through God's tender mercy, the Dayspring from on high has visited us, bringing light to people sitting in darkness.

God enlightens hearts so they receive his truth like clay receiving the impress of a seal (2 Corinthians 4:6).

God's way in governing the world is described as being in the sea—hidden from us.

If we are assured that the gates of heaven will open to us after death, we need not fear the gates of death.

Someone unable to measure even the breadth of the earth should not presume to search the full depths of God's counsel.

At the brightest noon, do not assume it will always be day.

At the darkest midnight, do not despair of morning's return.

This applies to our inward spiritual condition as well as outward circumstances.

How foolish to fight against God, when our greatest interest lies in making peace with him and remaining in his love!

Other mighty works and divine compassion (verses 25–41)

Earlier, God's questions exposed Job's ignorance.

Now they also exposed his weakness.

Knowing so little, Job should not put God's plans on trial.

Being able to accomplish so little, he should not oppose Providence.

The Lord's care is enough to satisfy the needs of every living creature.

He even feeds young ravens.

Surely he will not neglect his own people.

That example of compassion is only one among countless gifts God provides every day without our awareness.

Every glimpse of divine perfection should remind us that God deserves our love, that sin against him is evil, and that we need his mercy and salvation.

God teaches Job through animals

The Lord continued to humble Job through questions about the living creatures he had made.

The nature and circumstances of each animal reveal something of the power, wisdom and variety of God's works.

Consider the wild donkey.

It is better to work diligently and accomplish something useful than to wander without purpose and be of no use.

If Job could not command even the colt of a wild donkey, how unfit was he to issue instructions to divine Providence!

Henry also describes the powerful creature called the unicorn in his biblical witness.

It possesses the strength to perform useful service but is unwilling to do so.

God challenged Job to compel it to work.

When the Lord gives someone the strength to serve, it is a special mercy if he also gives a willing heart.

We should pray for that willingness and reason ourselves into it, because unlike animals we can reflect on our duty.

The most impressive-looking qualities are not always the most valuable gifts.

Henry contrasts the nightingale's song with the peacock's beautiful tail.

He would rather possess the eagle's eyesight and soaring wings, and the stork's parental affection, than the ostrich's fine feathers, since the ostrich cannot soar and appears to lack natural care for its young.

The description of the warhorse pictures presumptuous sinners.

As a horse rushes into battle, so people fully committed to evil hurry along the way their desires and passions have chosen.

They may refuse to fear the wrath of God and the fatal consequences of sin, however recklessly their desires drive them.

Some sinners believe themselves secure in their sin, like an eagle nesting high among inaccessible rocks.

But the Lord declares that even from such a height he can bring the proud down (Jeremiah 49:16).

Every wonderful image of animal life and behavior should teach us to honor the Creator's wisdom, which sustains everything he has made.

Job's failure to recognize how completely divine wisdom is present in God's works led him to speak in unworthy ways about Providence.

The wild ass. It is better to labour and be good for something, than to ramble and be good for nothing. From the untameableness of this and other creatures, we may see, how unfit we are to give law to Providence, who cannot give law even to a wild ass's colt. The description of the war-horse helps to explain the character of presumptuous sinners. Every one turneth to his course, as the horse rushes into the battle. When a man's heart is fully set in him to do evil, and he is carried on in a wicked way, by the violence of his appetites and passions, there is no making him fear the wrath of God, and the fatal consequences of sin. He can bring the sword of his justice and wrath against it.
